title: Jasper, Foundation 1
text_faithful: Revelation 21:19 names jasper first among the foundation stones: 'the first foundation was jasper.' The faith view records the order and the honour of first place; it does not settle which modern mineral the ancient name denoted.
engineering: Jasper in modern gemology is an opaque variety of chalcedony, a microcrystalline quartz coloured by iron oxides and other inclusions. A foundation course described as jasper is therefore, in engineering terms, a dense, opaque, polishable silica stone, not a transparent gem.
body:
History and description: Jasper has been cut, polished, and set since antiquity, used for seals, beads, vases, and wall facing. Red jasper coloured by hematite is the best known variety, but jasper occurs in yellow, brown, green, and banded patterns, so colour alone never identifies a historical jasper.

Science proof: Science proof: jasper is silicon dioxide, SiO2, in microcrystalline form, with Mohs hardness about 6.5 to 7 and a refractive index near 1.54. Its opacity comes from dense inclusions and fine grain scattering light rather than transmitting it, which is why a jasper slab reads as a solid coloured wall rather than a glowing window.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: from the refractive index, the critical angle for total internal reflection at a jasper-air boundary is arcsin(1/n). The demo computes it, showing why an opaque stone's surface behaviour is governed by polish and scattering, not by internal light return.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: established. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Sources: Sources: standard gemological references for jasper as microcrystalline quartz; Revelation 21:19 (short excerpt quoted in the faith view). Provenance: this public-edition record states established public facts, harvested from standard references.

import math
n = 1.54
crit = math.degrees(math.asin(1.0 / n))
print(f'jasper: refractive index {n}')
print(f'critical angle: {crit:.2f} degrees')
print('Mohs hardness: 6.5-7')
print('opacity: opaque, light scattered by inclusions')

critical angle: 40.49 degrees
Mohs hardness: 6.5-7
opacity: opaque, light scattered by inclusions

engineering: Sapphire is the gem variety of corundum, aluminium oxide, in every colour except red (red corundum is ruby). Blue sapphire, coloured by iron and titanium, is the classic stone, but the engineering facts are the corundum facts whatever the colour.
body:
History and description: Sapphire has been prized since antiquity and is now also an industrial material: watch crystals, optical windows, and substrates for light-emitting devices all use synthetic corundum, because the same hardness and clarity that suit a gem suit an engineering window.

Science proof: Science proof: corundum is Al2O3, Mohs hardness 9, refractive index about 1.76 to 1.77, with strong durability and chemical resistance. Its high hardness means a sapphire foundation facing would resist scratching far better than quartz stones, though its cost and crystal size limit any large-scale use.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: the demo computes the critical angle from n = 1.76 and compares it with quartz, showing that higher index narrows the escape cone and increases internal reflection, one reason sapphire shows strong brilliance.

engineering: Chalcedony is a microcrystalline quartz, typically translucent, waxy in lustre, and often pale blue-grey or white. Agate is its banded variety. In engineering terms it is a tough, fine-grained silica that takes a good polish and is workable at slab scale.
body:
History and description: Chalcedony was carved into seals, cameos, and vessels in the ancient world, and the name itself comes from Chalcedon, an ancient city. Science proof: Science proof: chalcedony is SiO2, Mohs hardness 6.5 to 7, refractive index near 1.53, specific gravity about 2.60. Its fibrous microcrystalline structure gives it toughness greater than single-crystal quartz of the same hardness, because cracks must cross many grain boundaries.

engineering: Sardonyx is banded chalcedony in which sard (reddish-brown) layers alternate with white or black onyx layers. body:

engineering: Modern topaz is a fluorine-bearing aluminium silicate, occurring colourless, yellow, blue, and pink. Blue topaz in the modern market is usually irradiated and heated colourless topaz, a treatment that is standard, disclosed in reputable trade, and stable.
body:

Science proof: Science proof: topaz is Al2SiO4(F,OH)2, Mohs hardness 8, refractive index about 1.62, specific gravity about 3.53. Its high density for a gem silicate is a useful identification check alongside optics.

title: Foundation Order Validator
text_faithful: The faith view for this record is procedural, not doctrinal: it checks that a proposed foundation list keeps the Revelation 21:19-20 order (jasper, sapphire, chalcedony, emerald, sardonyx, sardius, chrysolite, beryl, topaz, chrysoprasus, jacinth, amethyst) without adding, dropping, or reordering a stone.
engineering: The validator is a simple list-comparison program: it takes a candidate list of twelve names, compares it position by position with the reference order, and reports matches, mismatches, and missing or extra entries. It is established software practice applied to a fixed list; the list itself is textual, the comparison is mechanical.
body:
History and description: Order validators of this kind are routine in cataloguing: a checklist that fails loudly is more useful than a checklist that silently accepts a transposition. The history here is the history of the list's transmission, where copyist transpositions are a known hazard in any twelve-item sequence.

Science proof: Science proof, not applicable as laboratory science, with reason: the validator proves nothing about minerals; it proves a property of a list, namely exact-order equality. Its correctness is shown by testing, not by experiment: the demo runs it against the correct order, a swapped order, and a short list, and all three cases report correctly.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: the demo scores a candidate list as matches out of twelve, reports the first mismatch position, and flags length errors, giving a numeric audit trail for any foundation catalogue.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: integrated. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Sources: Sources: Revelation 21:19-20 for the reference order; this record's validator design is a Signature-generated completion for this suite, with provenance stated here. demo:
ORDER = ['jasper', 'sapphire', 'chalcedony', 'emerald', 'sardonyx', 'sardius', 'chrysolite', 'beryl', 'topaz', 'chrysoprasus', 'jacinth', 'amethyst']

def check(candidate):
    score = sum(1 for a, b in zip(candidate, ORDER) if a == b)
    first_bad = next((i + 1 for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(candidate, ORDER)) if a != b), None)
    return score, first_bad, len(candidate) == 12

for label, cand in [('correct', ORDER), ('swapped 2-3', [ORDER[0], ORDER[2], ORDER[1]] + ORDER[3:]), ('short', ORDER[:11])]:
    s, bad, ok_len = check(cand)
    print(f'{label}: matches {s}/12, first mismatch at {bad}, full length {ok_len}')
expected_output:
correct: matches 12/12, first mismatch at None, full length True
swapped 2-3: matches 10/12, first mismatch at 2, full length True
short: matches 11/12, first mismatch at None, full length False

title: Natural Versus Synthetic Comparator
text_faithful: The faith view does not distinguish natural from synthetic stones; the text names stones, not production methods. This record's distinction is entirely gemological and commercial, and it is kept separate from the faith view.
engineering: Natural stones formed geologically; synthetic stones are laboratory-grown with the same chemistry and crystal structure (flame-fusion, flux, hydrothermal, and high-pressure methods). Simulants, by contrast, merely look similar and differ chemically. The comparator keeps all three categories apart, because confusing synthetic with simulant is the commonest error in this field.
